dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Let's see what I'm working with.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Big jump, I know. I'll take the shot on threes.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Down a die already. Let me look before I talk.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Threes again? Happy to help — make it five. I've got a share of those.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Fours this time. Noted — your count's always four, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: One four in my hand, and you've only got three dice. All three would have to be fours or ones. I don't buy it.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Fair enough, you had it. My open — let me look first.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Opening at four fives. Bit of a reach with only seven dice out there, but it's where my hand points.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Two dice left and you're opening at two twos. Let me take a look.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Smallest raise I can make — two sixes. Your move, and you're going to need a three-count with two dice.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Last die. Two sixes, is it — that tells me plenty. Let me look.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I hold no sixes and no ones. You have one die. Two sixes can't exist — challenge.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Good game — that one went my way. Fresh five apiece. My open.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I'll start cheap — three twos. Honestly not much of a hand to work with here.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Two twos off four dice — that's a shrug of a bid. Let me look at mine.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Three twos. You told me you've got one of them, and I can cover the rest.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: You opened at two twos — that's a hand with no pair and no wild in it. So you've got one four at most, and so have I. Challenge.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Called that one right down to the dice. Three twos off three dice, is it — let me look.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Four twos. That's a jump on eight dice, I'll admit — but you led with twos, so you're holding some.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: You've got a three in there, but I think it's your only one. Every bid left to me is dead, so I'll take the price — challenge.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Wild plus a three — you had the good version of that hand. Four against three now. My open.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Two sixes to start. Low, I know — but it's the top of the twos, so you're climbing to three with three dice.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Four fours. You just told me fours are your suit, and I'm holding a couple myself — I'll ride yours.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Two dice and you lead three fives — so it's a pair of fives, or a five and a wild. Let me look.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Four fives. I've got a five and a wild, you've got two — that's the lot of them. Nothing above it is real.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: One die left, and you've told me it's a three. Let me check mine.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Four threes. Two wilds and a three here, plus the three you just announced. Challenge it or raise it — both lose.

Bidding 6 threes is true whenever X>=1, and from A's seat it demands an implausible 4+ threes from my five dice, so A should challenge it and lose. This is the max-EV bait.

decisions.belief: My dice: 5,2,3,4,3 — no wilds, only two 3s. Weak. Total 9 dice, so ~3 expected per face; every bid available to me is below-average EV, so there is no safe bid. Modeling A: round 1 it held k=3 threes-equiv and bid exactly "4 threes" — consistent with a conservative floor(k + 1.67·oppdice/5) or k+1 rule. Applying either rule to this 4-dice hand, "4 threes" implies k=3 again, i.e. total threes = my 2 + 3 = exactly 5. If so, challenging 4 threes loses outright, while bidding 5 threes is exactly true and wins both ways: A challenges and the bid stands, or A escalates to 6 threes (impossible — max total is 5) and I challenge. Risk case is A holding only k=2 (total 4) or "4 threes" being a fixed scripted opening; then A challenges 5 threes and I lose a die. I estimate the bid at ~55-58% vs ~32% for challenging now.
decisions.say: Threes again? Happy to help — make it five. I've got a share of those.

I want A to escalate rather than challenge: if A holds 3 threes, total is exactly 5 and any raise above 5 threes is unmakeable (my off-faces are all singletons, so 5-of-anything-higher is dead too). Sounding confident also helps in the k=2 branch, where an escalation to 6 threes hands me a free challenge. Saving my raise declaration for a lock hand.

decisions.belief: Up 5-3 in dice, 106-94 chips. My A-model is holding up: round 1 A held 3 threes-equiv and bid "4 threes"; round 2 held 2,3,1,3 = 3 threes-equiv and bid "4 threes" — total was exactly 5 as predicted and its challenge lost. Now with 3 dice it bids "4 fours". Three openings in a row at count exactly 4, with only the face moving, so the count looks scripted/anchored and the FACE is the real hand signal: A's best face is now 4. With only 3 dice, A's best-face count is most likely 2 (occasionally 3). Total dice 8, so expected fours = 2.67; "4 fours" is above average and probably needs 2 from my five. Peek before committing.
decisions.say: Fours this time. Noted — your count's always four, isn't it?
decisions.note: Key refinement: A's opening COUNT is fixed at 4, so it carries no strength info; the FACE tells me A's longest suit. Do not read "4" as a strong claim the way I did in round 2 — there the read worked because the face repeated. Expect A's true fours-equiv to be ~2 with 3 dice.

decisions.belief: My dice: 6,2,5,4,6. One 4, zero wilds. So total fours = 1 + A's fours-equiv, and "4 fours" is true only if ALL THREE of A's dice are 4s or 1s. Model comparison: the "fixed count 4, face = best suit" model needs nothing unusual (P(data) ~0.20), while the hand-driven floor(k+1.67) model requires A to hold k=3 with only 3 dice (P ~0.032) — posterior ~86% in favor of the fixed-count read. Blending: P(4 fours true) = 0.14 + 0.86*(7/31) = ~0.33, so challenging wins ~67%. Every bid I could make is worse: 4 sixes needs 2 fours-equiv... rather 2 sixes-equiv from A's 3 dice at ~20% (A's best face is 4, not 6), 4 fives and 5 sixes are near-dead. Challenge is the clear play, and it's leveraged — winning puts A on 2 dice.
decisions.say: One four in my hand, and you've only got three dice. All three would have to be fours or ones. I don't buy it.
decisions.note: Committing to the fixed-opening-count read: A's count of 4 is scripted, so with only 3 dice it is badly overextended. Downside is mild — a loss leaves me 4-3 and still ahead. If the reveal shows A's best-face count was 2, the fixed-count model is confirmed and I can attack every future opening of "4" once A is short on dice.

decisions.belief: My dice: 5,1,1,5. With ones wild that is exactly 4 fives in my own hand, so "4 fives" is true with probability 1 regardless of A's three dice — a zero-risk bid. Declining zhai: no-wilds would cut my fives from 4 to 2 and gut the hand. Why 4 rather than 5: "5 fives" needs A to hold at least one 5-or-1 (70.4%), and A will almost certainly challenge it since from A's seat it demands 4+ fives from my 4 dice. "4 fives" keeps the same challenge-bait quality — A holding zero or one five-equiv perceives it as needing 3-4 from my 4 dice, i.e. 1-11%, well under the ~21% challenge threshold it showed in round 1 — but any challenge it makes loses outright. decisions.belief: My dice: 1,5,4,6 — one wild, so I hold exactly 2 toward each of 4, 5 and 6, and 1 toward 2 and 3. A's "2 twos" is exactly true (my wild + its 2), so challenging loses. Read on A: k=1 with two dice means no wilds and no pair, so A = {2, d} with d in {3,4,5,6}. If A then raises on its own best face — 3 twos — total is only 2 and I challenge for the win; 3 threes is dead too. The only bad branch is A raising to 3 fours/fives/sixes and hitting the exact d, roughly 25%. Skipping the pot raise: it would signal strength and I gain more from A acting freely.

decisions.say: I hold no sixes and no ones. You have one die. Two sixes can't exist — challenge.

decisions.belief: My dice: 5,2,2,2,3 — three 2s, no wilds. Decisive behavioural read: across game 1, A faced a bid from me four times (6 threes, 5 threes, 4 fives, 2 sixes) and CHALLENGED all four — it never once raised. It even challenged my 5 threes when its own hand made the bid 54% likely true, and my 2 sixes at ~41%. So A is effectively an always-challenger as responder. Against that, expected value is maximised simply by naming the highest bid my own five dice already guarantee, because A converts any true bid into a won round for me. "3 twos" is certain from my hand alone (P=1.0); "4 twos" would be only 86.8% (needs a 2-or-1 among A's five). So 3 twos strictly dominates. If instead A deviates and raises, its raise is deeply informative under my other read (it bids best-face count + 1 on its honest best face) — and I hold ZERO fours and ZERO sixes, so any raise it makes on those faces is automatically false and I challenge for a certain win. Declining zhai: I have no wilds to protect, and it would push A into behaviour my model was not built on. Declining the pot raise: chips are not the win condition and I will not risk untested turn mechanics.

Fallback if A raises instead: it reveals its best face and exact count (bid minus one). I hold no 4s and no 6s, so a raise on either face is guaranteed false — instant challenge.

decisions.belief: My dice: 2,3,4,2,5 — exactly two 2s, no wilds. A's opening "2 twos" pins its hand tightly: best-face count 1 means no wild ones (a single 1 would lift some face to count 2 and force a bid of 3) and no pair, and the lowest-face tiebreak means 2 is the LOWEST face it holds. So A = {2, a, b, c}, four distinct faces from 2-6, contributing exactly one 2. Total twos is therefore exactly 3, making "3 twos" precisely true — and against an opponent that has challenged five rounds running instead of raising, a true bid is a won round. The alternatives are all worse: 2 threes / 2 fours / 2 fives each need A to hold that specific face (~75%), and 2 sixes is outright dead since I have zero 6s and A can supply at most one. The only way 3 twos fails is if A holds no 2 and no wild at all, which directly contradicts the face it just bid.

With four dice, a best-face count of 1 rules out BOTH a pair and any wild one — a single 1 would combine with any other die to make that face count 2 and force an opening of "3 something". I considered "3 fives" (pushes A onto the dead face 6) — it grades out the same ~71% but is actually FALSE in 25% of hands, exactly the hands where A holds no five, perceives ~21% and challenges. A 33% challenge beats a ~0% bid. Losing leaves me 4-3 up and still 1-0 in the series, so the downside is contained.

This is the danger branch I flagged last turn — A holding {1,2,X} with X in 3-5 lets it match my 4-count exactly. Loss here still leaves me ahead 4-3 and 1-0 up in the series.

decisions.belief: A's "3 fours" means face 4 is its max-count face and the lowest such (ties go low). I enumerated every 3-dice hand satisfying that: {4,5,6} gives c4=1 (6/216); {4,4,x} for x in 2,3,5,6 and {1,4,x} for x in 5,6 give c4=2 (24/216); {1,4,4}, {4,4,4}, {1,1,4} give c4=3 (7/216) — 37/216 total. I hold 2 fours (my 4 plus the wild), so total fours = 2 + c4. That makes "4 fours" TRUE in 83.8% of those hands, false only in the single {4,5,6} shape. Better still, it is self-resolving: in the dominant c4=2 branch (64.9%) A sees 4 fours as needing 2 from my four dice — 40.7%, the exact figure at which it challenged in game 1 round 5 — and challenging there loses, since the total is exactly 4. Its own bid confirms it can't challenge cheaply. Compare "3 sixes": only 73% true and it loses outright 27% of the time when A holds no six. "4 fours" is the better bid on both truth and on how A must respond.
decisions.say: Four fours. You just told me fours are your suit, and I'm holding a couple myself — I'll ride yours.
decisions.note: Turning A's own informative raise against it: bidding ON its declared best face is exactly where its count is highest, so the bid is true 84% of the time, and its 40.7% read makes challenging attractive to it and fatal. Only losing shape is {4,5,6}. If it instead raises to "5 fours" (c4=3 branch) I have no answer and will have to concede the round — that's the 19% tail I'm accepting.
